steps.line: New York, 1922. A twelve-year-old named Judith Kaplan wakes up on a Saturday morning, a little nervous.
Boys became bar mitzvah, “son of the commandment,” and marked it by reading from the Torah in synagogue. In most synagogues, girls had no ceremony like it.

steps.q: Judith’s father is the rabbi there, and he calls her up to read. How do you guess she reads?
o: From the Torah scroll, as boys did
From a printed book, not the scroll
From her seat among the women
steps.why: From her own printed Bible, a little apart from the scroll, once the week’s regular reading was done. Watch how people took it.

steps.line: Her father, Rabbi Mordecai Kaplan, called her up. She said the blessings and read the week’s passage aloud, from a printed book, a little apart from the scroll.
It became known as the first public bat mitzvah in America: “daughter of the commandment.” Some people were thrilled. Some were shocked.

steps.q: Years later, Judith described that morning. What did she remember?
o: No thunder sounded, no lightning struck
She cried all the way through
The whole room stood up and cheered
steps.why: Her words, decades later: “No thunder sounded, no lightning struck.” The rest of the day, she said, was all rejoicing.

steps.line: Today, in many synagogues, girls and boys read from the scroll itself. In many Orthodox communities, a bat mitzvah is marked in other ways, like a talk or a celebration.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Judith read from a printed book, a little apart from the scroll. Why might her father have set it up that way?
o: A big change, made one careful step at a time
Girls weren’t taught to read Hebrew then
The scroll was too heavy for her to hold
steps.why: Many historians see it as a careful first step. Within a few decades, girls in many synagogues were reading from the scroll itself.

steps.line: And some people mark it as adults, at thirty, sixty, even eighty. There’s no deadline.
steps.label: today

steps.q: In traditional Jewish law, a girl becomes bat mitzvah at twelve, a year before a boy. Why?
o: The sages held that girls mature earlier
A girl’s ceremony was always smaller
steps.why: The Talmud says girls reach maturity sooner; one sage even reads Genesis as giving women extra understanding. Many communities now mark both at thirteen.

say: here’s what i love. the ceremony didn’t make judith a bat mitzvah. her birthday did. the ceremony just said it out loud, for a girl, for the first time there.
in jewish tradition, until that age your parents carry the responsibility. from then on, the mitzvot, the commandments, are yours. how a community marks it differs; the responsibility is the same.

steps.q: A woman of seventy has her bat mitzvah. From this lesson, what is she celebrating?
o: Becoming bat mitzvah for the first time
Something true since she turned twelve
steps.why: The responsibility came with her twelfth birthday, ceremony or not. Like Judith, she’s saying it out loud, in front of everyone.

today.say: do one mitzvah on purpose today. an easy, real one: call or visit someone who’s sick or alone. in jewish tradition that’s a mitzvah called bikur cholim, visiting the sick.
options: that’s a mitzvah. it’s yours now.
that counts. a mitzvah done on purpose is the whole idea.

sources: Judith Kaplan Eisenstein’s bat mitzvah, 18 March 1922, Society for the Advancement of Judaism, New York (Jewish Women’s Archive)
Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 45b (the ages of adulthood: twelve for a girl, thirteen for a boy)
Genesis Rabbah 63:10 (a father’s responsibility until thirteen)
check: ‘First public bat mitzvah in America’ is the standard claim; earlier girls’ ceremonies existed elsewhere
Orthodox practice described generally (a talk, learning or celebration; in most Orthodox communities girls do not read from the Torah publicly)
Some people were ‘thrilled’, some ‘shocked’: general reaction, no specific report quoted
